title: Not All Rural Areas Are Created Equal: State and Regional Variation in the US Rural–Urban Health Gap in the Year 2025
content: Background: Rural–urban health gaps in the United States are usually reported as a single national number, which hides large variation between states and regions. Methods: We used the 2025 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (356,158 adults; 276,884 with complete data on age, sex, education and income, of whom 37,237 lived in rural areas). Within each state and Census region we estimated the rural–urban difference in fair or poor self-rated health, unadjusted, adjusted for age and sex, and further adjusted for education and income, using design-based linear probability models. States were ranked on each model. We repeated the unadjusted comparison for 15 indicators (education, income, smoking, hypertension, obesity, diabetes, inactivity, depression, mental distress, insurance, cost barriers, life satisfaction and loneliness). The share of the age–sex gap attributable to socioeconomic status (SES) was estimated with a Rao–Wu rescaled bootstrap. Results: Nationally, rural adults reported fair or poor health more often than urban adults (22.9% vs 18.5%; difference 4.4 points, 95% CI 3.4–5.4); the gap was 3.5 points after age and sex adjustment and 0.2 points (−0.8 to 1.1) after SES adjustment. The gap was largest in the South (6.2 points) and was close to zero or negative in every region after SES adjustment except the South. Among 40 ranked states, 37 showed a rural excess unadjusted (17 statistically significant), led by New Hampshire (18.2), Arizona (12.8), Alabama (11.7), Virginia (10.3) and West Virginia (9.8). After SES adjustment only New Hampshire and West Virginia retained a clear excess. SES accounted for at least half of the age–sex gap in 28 states, and in 11 states the gap reversed sign. No state showed a statistically clear rural advantage before SES adjustment; Washington did after it. Rural disadvantage in education was universal, in income, hypertension, smoking and inactivity near-universal, whereas depression, mental distress, insurance and life satisfaction showed no consistent rural excess. Conclusions: Rural health disadvantage is not one phenomenon. It is concentrated in the South and a few states, is largely SES-linked in most places, and differs by indicator. State-specific rural strategies are warranted.
